p01.why: get is noexcept and other has no specifier, so it is potentially throwing; both assertions hold.

p02.why: A call through a pointer to a non-throwing function is non-throwing; the call is never evaluated.

p03.why: A program-written function without a specifier is potentially throwing.

p04.why: The operand can name g, declared later in the class, and g is noexcept.

p05.why: The defaulted and implicit special members of S touch only an int, so they are non-throwing.

p06.why: The two declarations differ only in noexcept.

p07.why: Plain's destructor is noexcept by DTOR-4, so delete p is non-throwing; Risky's destructor is noexcept(false).

p08.why: Inherited constructors keep the specifier of the base constructor.

p09.why: Each specialization gets its own specifier: store<char> is throwing, store<double> is noexcept, and copy_of follows the copy constructor of T.

p10.why: A destructor that overrides a noexcept destructor must be noexcept.

p11.why: A defaulted function can state its own specifier.

p12.why: Clang and GCC accept throw() as noexcept, and EDG rejects it.

p13.why: noexcept is part of the function type, of function pointers, and of member function pointers.

p14.why: A lambda is non-throwing only with noexcept.

p15.why: The operand depends on f's own specifier; GCC and EDG accept, and Clang rejects.

p16.why: The operand can use the parameter x, and x + 1 does not throw.

p17.why: The defaulted == compares only an int, so it is non-throwing.

p18.why: No use needs the specifier of Box<int>::put, and the call store(1) picks the plain function over the template, so the template's specifier is never needed.

p19.why: The noexcept operator needs put's specifier, and int::safe is not valid.

p20.why: Both overloads are viable; the noexcept parameter needs no dropping of noexcept, so its sequence is a proper subsequence and wins.

p21.why: All operands are constant expressions with the stated values.

p22.why: The defaulted constructor calls M's potentially throwing constructor.

p23.why: The evidence says the compilers treat the placement new as non-throwing; Whole() also runs the potentially throwing destructor of the temporary.

p24.why: decltype keeps noexcept in the function type and the pointer type.

p25.why: Clang and EDG treat a class-specific operator delete as non-throwing; GCC treats it as potentially throwing and rejects the assertion.

p26.why: The call needs put's specifier, and int::safe is not valid.

p27.why: A typedef keeps noexcept, and Fn f declares a function.

p28.why: Clang and GCC treat the defaulted == as potentially throwing, so the assertion holds; EDG treats it as non-throwing and the assertion fails.

p29.why: Deleting an int calls no destructor, and the deallocation function is non-throwing.

p30.why: A pointer operand narrows to bool; EDG accepts, and Clang and GCC reject.

p31.why: The override of a noexcept virtual function is not noexcept.

p32.why: flag is not a constant expression.

p33.why: An override can be noexcept when the base function is not.

p34.why: throw with a list of types is not valid.

p35.why: constexpr does not make a function non-throwing.

p36.why: The alias keeps noexcept, work converts to the pointer, and the call increments calls to 1.

p37.why: The implicit constructors of S call M's potentially throwing constructors.

p38.why: The two declarations differ only in noexcept.

p39.why: noexcept is kept in pointers to functions at any depth and in arrays of them.

p40.why: The default member initializer calls may_throw, so the implicit constructor is potentially throwing.

p41.why: 2 narrows to bool; EDG accepts, and Clang and GCC reject.
